t: Check ASCII Palindromic — Build and Compare
o: Convert each lowercase letter to its 8-bit binary ASCII representation (with leading zeros), concatenate in order, and test whether the resulting bit string reads the same forwards and backwards. Since each byte is fixed-width, the concatenation length is 8*len(s) <= 800 — trivially small. Example "ff" gives 01100110 repeated, a palindrome; "leet" does not. Note the palindrome is over the whole bit string, not per character, so mixed strings generally fail even if each byte alone were symmetric.
k: Fixed-width 8-bit encoding makes construction a simple format-and-concatenate step.
The palindrome check applies to the entire concatenated bit string, not individual bytes.
Length is at most 800, so any direct method works.

a.n: Approach 1: Construct Bit String, Then Two-Pointer Palindrome Check
a.i: Format each character as an 8-bit zero-padded binary string, join them, then verify palindromicity with two pointers moving inward from both ends.
s: Build t by appending format(ord(c), '08b') for each character c.
While left < right, if t[left] != t[right] return false; move pointers inward.
a.t: O(n) — building the 8n-length string and scanning it once.
a.sp: O(n) — the constructed bit string (could be O(1) extra with index arithmetic mapping bit positions back to characters).

a.n: Approach 2: Virtual Index Comparison Without Building the String
a.i: Bit position p in the virtual string corresponds to character p/8 and bit (7 - p%8) of its ASCII value. Compare positions p and L-1-p directly, avoiding materialization — useful if memory were constrained or the string were streamed.
s: Let L = 8 * len(s). Define bit(p) = (ord(s[p/8]) >> (7 - p%8)) & 1.
For p from 0 to L/2 - 1, compare bit(p) with bit(L-1-p).
Return false on any mismatch, true otherwise.
a.t: O(n) — checks 4n bit pairs, each O(1).

w: Either approach is fine given the tiny constraints; the constructive version is easier to explain and debug, the virtual-index version shows bit-manipulation fluency. Pitfalls: dropping leading zeros (must be exactly 8 bits per char), checking per-byte palindromes instead of the full string, and sign issues when shifting chars in Java/C++ (chars here are ASCII so safe). Follow-up: determine which single-character edits make s palindromic, or handle Unicode code points.
